title: The Digital Native Myth

hooks.text: Is your tech fluency a birthright?
You think it is age. The evidence says it is literacy.

A thumb moves across a glass screen.

reveal.headline: The evidence does not compare adoption speeds.
reveal.body: There is no data provided to prove whether older adults or teenagers adopt platform mechanics faster. The research focuses on literacy, demographics, and well-being.

explain.headline: Access depends on your life circumstances.
explain.body: Internet access is linked to your age, education, income, and social isolation. Digital well-being is tied to literacy skills rather than just age or platform familiarity.

matters.headline: Digital skill is not an innate trait.
matters.body: That may be why some people struggle with technology. It is not a generational gift. It is a result of your social support, your income, and your specific literacy needs.

example.headline: A dinner table with three phones.
example.body: You watch your parents struggle to navigate a new app while you scroll effortlessly. You assume it is a lack of speed. The evidence suggests it is a lack of specific literacy or support.

verdict: The provided sources do not contain data comparing the speed of platform adoption between older adults and teenagers.
caveat: None of the sources provide comparative data on the rate of adaptation to social media interfaces between different age groups.
caption:
The myth of the digital native ignores the underlying structures of access. 

Research shows that internet access and digital well-being are linked to demographics like income, education, and social isolation. The evidence does not provide data comparing the speed of platform adoption between different age groups.

Does your environment shape your digital habits more than your age?
